summary: This standards-track RFC defines how clients of SMTP Submission, IMAP, POP and ManageSieve check a server's identity when using TLS. It replaces a section of RFC 2595 and updates RFC 3207, RFC 3501 and RFC 5804.

eli5.summary: Before telling an email server your secrets, you check its name tag matches who you think it is. This explains how.

subtitle: One consistent rule for how email clients decide that the server behind a TLS connection is really the one they meant to reach.

tldr.problem: SMTP Submission, IMAP, POP and ManageSieve each described slightly different rules for checking a server's TLS certificate, or none at all, even though the same developers implement them together.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7817 gives one procedure: build reference identifiers from the user's email domain and the host name used, then match them against the certificate using the rules of RFC 6125, plus supplemental rules for DNS-ID, SRV-ID, CN-ID and wildcards.
tldr.outcome: It replaces a section of RFC 2595 and updates RFC 3207, RFC 3501 and RFC 5804, and it also tells CAs and mail providers what certificates must contain.

today: RFC 7817 is a Proposed Standard, and neither obsoleted nor updated by a later RFC according to the unit metadata. It updates RFC 2595, RFC 3207, RFC 3501 and RFC 5804.

sections.title: Why One Identity Check
sections.content:
Use of TLS by SMTP Submission, IMAP, POP and ManageSieve clients is described in four different documents: RFC 3207, RFC 3501, RFC 2595 and RFC 5804. Each describes slightly different rules for checking the server certificate's identity, or defines no rules at all.

Email client and server developers usually implement several of these protocols together, so the RFC defines modern and consistent rules. Section 3 of RFC 7817 replaces Section 2.4 of RFC 2595. The document does not apply to TLS used between mail servers (MTA-to-MTA SMTP).
sections.eli5: Four mail programs each had their own way of checking a server's name tag. This RFC picks one way so everyone checks the same.

sections.title: Reference Identifiers and Identifier Types
sections.content:
A reference identifier is a domain name that the email client associates with the server it wants to reach. The client compares these against the identities in the server's certificate. The term comes from RFC 6125.

The certificate can carry a name in several forms:

  • DNS-ID: a subjectAltName entry of type dNSName.
  • SRV-ID: a subjectAltName entry of type otherName whose name form is SRVName.
  • URI-ID: a subjectAltName entry of type uniformResourceIdentifier with a scheme and a host.
  • CN-ID: a Common Name attribute in the certificate subject that looks like a domain name.
sections.eli5: A certificate can list its name in a few different boxes on the name tag. You need to know which boxes exist before you can read them.

sections.title: How a Client Verifies the Server
sections.content:
During the TLS negotiation, an email client MUST compare its reference identifiers with the identity in the server's Certificate message, to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. The check happens only after the certificate passes certification path validation as described in Section 6 of RFC 5280. Matching follows Section 6 of RFC 6125, including the order in which identifier types are tried, certificate pinning, and what to do on a mismatch.

For DNS-ID and CN-ID matching, the client MUST use one or more of these as reference identifiers: the domain part of the user's email address, or the host name used to open the connection (without CNAME canonicalization). It MAY also use a value securely derived from either, such as the result of a DNSSEC-validated lookup.

When the client uses the email service discovery procedure of RFC 6186, it MUST also use the domain part of the user's email address as a reference identifier to compare against an SRV-ID in the certificate.
sections.eli5: The mail program first checks that the name tag is genuine, then checks the name on it against the address you typed or the place you called. If they do not match, it does not trust the server.

sections.title: Supplemental Matching Rules
sections.content:
On top of RFC 6125, Section 3 adds five rules for email server certificates:

  • Support for DNS-ID is REQUIRED in email clients.
  • Support for SRV-ID is REQUIRED for clients that support RFC 6186. For ManageSieve the service name sieve is used.
  • Clients MUST NOT use URI-ID for server verification, because URI-IDs were not historically used for email.
  • For backward compatibility with deployed software, CN-ID MAY be used.
  • A * wildcard MAY be used as the left-most name component of a DNS-ID or CN-ID. *.example.com would match a.example.com and foo.example.com but not example.com. The wildcard MUST NOT be a fragment of the left-most component, so *oo.example.com, f*o.example.com and foo*.example.com are not allowed.
sections.eli5: The rules say which boxes on the name tag a mail program must read, which it must never read, and that a star can stand in for one whole first word of a name but not for part of a word.

sections.title: What CAs and Mail Providers Must Do
sections.content:
Certification Authorities MUST support issuing server certificates with a DNS-ID, with an SRV-ID for each type of email service, and, for backward compatibility, with a CN-ID. They MAY allow a wildcard as the left-most component. A CA that cannot verify that a requester is authorized to run email service for a domain MUST NOT include email SRV-IDs or DNS-IDs for it. A CA willing to sign a certificate with a DNS-ID SHOULD also support the email SRV-IDs for the same domain, since an SRV-ID gives more restricted access than a DNS-ID.

Mail Service Providers and certificate signing request tools MUST include a DNS-ID for the host names where email servers run, and SHOULD include one for the domain part of served addresses. They MUST include an SRV-ID for each email service that is discoverable through DNS SRV. They SHOULD include a CN-ID for the host name, noting that a certificate can have only one CN-ID.

Section 4.1 explains why SRV-IDs matter for delegated hosting: if a client connects to imap.hosting.example.net for an address at example.org, the certificate needs an SRV-ID or DNS-ID for example.org, or users would have to confirm exceptions manually.
sections.eli5: The people who make name tags (CAs) and the mail companies who ask for them must put the right names on the tag, and the CAs must check the company really runs mail for that name.

sections.title: Hosting Many Domains
sections.content:
A server hosting multiple domains needs to do one of the following, or a combination:

  • Use DNS SRV records to redirect each hosted service to a fixed domain, and have users configure pinning (unless SRV records can always be obtained via DNSSEC).
  • Use a single certificate listing every domain served.
  • Serve each domain on its own IP and port with separate certificates.
  • Use the Server Name Indication (SNI) TLS extension from RFC 6066 so each domain has its own certificate.

Each choice has scaling drawbacks when the domain list changes. The RFC states that it and its predecessors do not address scaling issues in multi-tenanted environments, and that further work is needed, possibly using DNSSEC or PKIX over Secure HTTP (POSH, RFC 7711).
sections.eli5: A mail company serving lots of names has to give each name its own tag or one big tag listing all the names. Both ways get awkward as the list grows.

sections.title: Certificate Examples
sections.content:
For an IMAP server at mail.example.net serving user@example.net, the certificate needs DNS-IDs of example.net and mail.example.net, and might carry a CN-ID of mail.example.net. If the service is also discoverable by DNS SRV records, it also needs SRV-IDs of _imap.example.net (STARTTLS on the IMAP port) and _imaps.example.net (TLS on the IMAPS port). Unlike DNS SRV, an SRV-ID has no _tcp component.

An SMTP Submission server at submit.example.net needs an SRV-ID of _submission.example.net with DNS-IDs of example.net and submit.example.net. A host running Submission, IMAPS, POP3S and ManageSieve can share one certificate with SRV-IDs _submission.example.net, _imaps.example.net, _pop3s.example.net and _sieve.example.net.
sections.eli5: The examples show filled-in name tags: which names a mail server's tag should list so that both people typing the address and programs looking up the server find a match.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The goal is to improve interoperability, and so security, by giving providers, client writers and CAs one set of rules. The check depends on trustworthy DNS host names being used as reference identifiers. Such names are either entered manually (for example, advertised on a provider's website), explicitly confirmed by the user (for example, the target of a DNS SRV lookup), or derived from a secure third party service such as DNSSEC-protected SRV records.

The RFC says future work might benefit from integration with DANE (RFC 6698), but that is not covered here. Appendix A lists the exact replacement text for the affected sections of RFC 2595, RFC 3207, RFC 3501 and RFC 5804. For ManageSieve, when the reference identity is an IP address, the client SHOULD compare against the iPAddress subjectAltName.
sections.eli5: The check is only as good as the name you start with. If a stranger tricks you into a wrong name, the check cannot help, so the name must come from a source you trust.
